messages.subject: pushed varying step size + reporting
parts:
I added reporting for step size in each iteration
to the Stan CSV output. We'll probably need to do a bit
more to get that neatly through to R.

I also added a report (as a comment line in the output)
for the adapted step size in all the samplers,
and for the diagonal mass matrix for nuts_diag.

I had to add varying step sizes to nuts and nuts_diag.
I only vary the step sizes after warmup/adaptation.

I also realized we don't have a way to print out the
warmup samples, step sizes, etc., in the runs from C++.
I'll work on that.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pushed varying step size + reporting
parts:
Oh, and I forgot to mention that the behavior is what
you expect (so far I've only looked at the Beetles model
as we're still trying to debug it). When the step size
varies by a large percentage, you start to see deeper
trees being generated by NUTS for the lower step sizes.

I've attached a plot of rejects vs. step size and
tree depth (log2 # leapfrog steps) vs. step size.

How should we draw these kinds of things? The way I
did it should be filed as a counterexample. Faceted
side by side are hard to interpret, but if I could stack
them vertically it'd look OK -- I find ggplot2 really
hard to control even though I've read the book and get
the basic patterns.

NUTS tuning is pretty impressive. 67% accept rate.
And the accept rate's higher for lower step sizes.
And you see a very clear relationship between step size
and number of steps.

This geometry stuff really seems to work!

Stan is really fast now! 0.2s w. clang++ -O0
for 2000 iterations with data read, output write,
and adaptation. I don't have the patience for a
g++ -O3 run (it's not so much the model as the libs,
which take forever to compile on my notebook).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pushed varying step size + reporting
parts:
On 7/2/12 10:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> instead of saving 1/0 accept/reject, we
> should be saving Pr(accept) at each step.
> This contains slightly more information.

For what I reported, I just used the Coda trick of
checking if the parameters were the same iteration
to iteration -- I haven't saved anything yet.

For HMC, there's a straightforward Metropolis step
based on the new probability.

In NUTS, it's not so clear what I should report.

First, there's a slice variable u, which is sampled
between 0 and the current probability uniformly (if you
look at the code, it's all done on the log scale; Radford
discusses this in his paper with analysis of probability [aka
energy] change).

Then, points in the NUTS tree generated by leapfrog
steps are rejected if their probability is below the
slice variable. The only way we get a full rejection is
if every leapfrog step produces parameters with probability
below the slice variable. I suppose something like the max
of those might be a good proxy.

Overall, Matt's code's surprisingly easy to read.
If you're looking at the code, there's a very clever online
test to update the point that will be the next sample each
tree expansion step. It's an instance of a general trick
to generate a random element from an array presented one
element at a time that you can't buffer.

- Bob
